edits.before: <para id="import-auto-id1169737779858"><term id="import-auto-id1169738218659">Gluons</term> (<m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>g</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{g} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>) are the proposed carrier particles for the strong nuclear force, although they are not directly observed. Like quarks, gluons may be confined to systems having a total color of white. Less is known about gluons than the fact that they are the carriers of the weak and certainly of the electromagnetic force. QCD theory calls for eight gluons, all massless and all spin 1. Six of the gluons carry a color and an anticolor, while two do not carry color, as illustrated in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169737711152"/>(a). There is indirect evidence of the existence of gluons in nucleons. When high-energy electrons are scattered from nucleons and evidence of quarks is seen, the momenta of the quarks are smaller than they would be if there were no gluons. That means that the gluons carrying force between quarks also carry some momentum, inferred by the already indirect quark momentum measurements. At any rate, the gluons carry color charge and can change the colors of quarks when exchanged, as seen in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169737711152"/>(b). In the figure, a red down quark interacts with a green strange quark by sending it a gluon. That gluon carries red away from the down quark and leaves it green, because it is an <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>R</m:mi><m:mover accent="true"><m:mi>G</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="true">¯</m:mo></m:mover></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{R { bar  {G}}} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> (red-antigreen) gluon. (Taking antigreen away leaves you green.) Its antigreenness kills the green in the strange quark, and its redness turns the quark red.</para>
edits.after:
<para id="import-auto-id1169737779858"><term id="import-auto-id1169738218659">Gluons</term> (<m:math><m:mi>g</m:mi></m:math>) are the experimentally established carriers of the strong interaction between quarks. Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) describes eight types of gluons, all massless and with spin 1. Gluons carry color charge and can interact with one another. Like quarks, they are confined within color-neutral combinations and are not observed as isolated particles. Their existence is established through experiments, including collisions that produce three jets of particles, corresponding to a quark, an antiquark, and a gluon.</para>
<para id="gluon-color-exchange-description">Gluon exchange can change a quark’s color without changing its flavor. In <link target-id="import-auto-id1169737711152"/>(b), a red down quark emits a red–antigreen gluon and becomes green. A green strange quark absorbs that gluon and becomes red. The quarks remain a down quark and a strange quark throughout the interaction.</para>

edits.before: <caption>In figure (a), the eight types of gluons that carry the strong nuclear force are divided into a group of six that carry color and a group of two that do not. Figure (b) shows that the exchange of gluons between quarks carries the strong force and may change the color of a quark.</caption>
edits.after: <caption>(a) The eight gluon color states can be represented by six unmatched color–anticolor combinations and two independent quantum superpositions of matched color–anticolor combinations. The two states shown as white circles are not color singlets; the “White” label in this schematic is misleading. (b) A red down quark and a green strange quark exchange a red–antigreen gluon, exchanging colors while retaining their flavors.</caption>
